clue.text: Mostly saves for a long time then tears to pieces

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all of the word is kept, so its tail end is cut off

blocks.note: taken as written before its ending is trimmed
'for ages' means for a long time

explanation.surface: Someone hoards things for ages and then rips them up in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'mostly' drops the last two letters of saves, leaving SAV, a little more than the usual single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To savage something is to attack it ferociously, mauling or ripping it apart, as a dog might.

clue.text: Agreed ladettes removed a drunk

indicators.note: something removed is taken away, so the single letter named next is struck out of the word
a drunk person staggers about, so the remaining letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; ladettes are rowdy young women
the letter to be taken out

explanation.surface: A group of boisterous young women agree that one of them, having had too much, should be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladette is British slang for a young woman who behaves loudly and drinks heavily. Take the A out of it before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter that is settled has been decided or resolved, with all parties in accord.

clue.text: Offer to work for no money

blocks.note: first meaning: to put yourself forward for a task
second meaning: to do a job unpaid, as a charity helper does

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase, an offer to work unpaid, but the verb and the description of unpaid labour are two separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To volunteer is both to offer your services freely and to do unpaid work as a helper.

clue.text: Overeat Cheddar?

definitions.note: an example: Cheddar Gorge, not a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: to stuff yourself with food
second meaning: a famous limestone ravine in Somerset, England

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether eating too much cheese counts as overindulging.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar looks like the cheese, tying in with overeating, but it is the village whose deep ravine, Cheddar Gorge, is a well-known English landmark; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to eat greedily to excess, and a gorge is a steep narrow valley such as the one at Cheddar.

clue.text: Saint gagged and put on the rack

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for saint
gagged in the sense of heaved, almost vomited

explanation.surface: A martyred saint is silenced and tortured.
explanation.walkthrough: Gagged suggests being silenced with a cloth, but here it means retching.
explanation.definitionFit: The rack was a torture device that pulled a victim's limbs, so someone put on it was pulled out lengthways.

clue.text: Smallest skirt for mother

blocks.note: a mini is a very short skirt
British informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Someone picks out the tiniest skirt as a present for their mother.
explanation.definitionFit: The minimum is the least possible amount, so it serves as an adjective meaning least or lowest.

clue.text: Sentimental about peas?

definitions.note: describes the peas rather than meaning them

blocks.note: first meaning: soppy, overly emotional
second meaning: the word that goes before peas in a British side dish of mashed marrowfat peas

explanation.surface: Someone gets weepy and emotional about a dish of peas.
explanation.walkthrough: Mushy peas are a British chip-shop side dish of soft mashed peas; the question mark signals the answer describes the peas.
explanation.definitionFit: Soppy, cloying emotion is often called mushy, and soft pulped peas are literally so.

clue.text: Story turned into rant on air

indicators.note: turned means twisted around, so the letters that follow are put in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tale turns into an angry tirade when a broadcaster goes on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A narration is a spoken or written account of events, the telling of a tale.

clue.text: Majority accept Matilda is slightly wet

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the first word holds the second within it

blocks.note: the most is the greater part
Matilda is the setter, who refers to herself as I

explanation.surface: Most people agree that Matilda is a bit damp.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming herself in a clue stands for I or ME; Matilda is this puzzle's setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Moist describes something lightly damp, holding a little water without being soaked.

clue.text: Game editor suited

blocks.note: a match is a game or contest
standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A games editor approves something as fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are matched go well together, so they are suited to each other.

clue.text: In brochure: literature about someone who works with walls and floors

definitions.text: someone who works with walls and floors

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows
about means turned round, so the concealed letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: concealed across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A trade brochure carries reading matter about a tradesman who finishes walls and floors.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiler is a tradesperson who lays ceramic tiles on walls, floors and bathroom surfaces.

clue.text: Control coach interfering with others

indicators.note: something interfering with a thing gets into the middle of it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: the rest are the others
to coach is to train

explanation.surface: Discipline is needed when a sports coach meddles with the other players.
explanation.walkthrough: Coach looks like a noun, a trainer or a bus, but works as the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is the act of holding back or keeping something in check, which is control.

clue.text: Gently unravel line, gently cutting top

indicators.note: cutting the top lops off the head, so the opening letter is dropped
to unravel is to undo and tangle loose, so the letters come apart and regroup

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then beheaded

explanation.surface: Instructions for carefully untangling a line, like fishing line, and trimming the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Gently' is the definition; the second loses its G and joins line in the letter mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting leniently means treating someone mildly and without harshness, which is gentle treatment.

clue.text: Don't drop this letter!

blocks.note: surface reading: a warning not to let a piece of post fall
setter's reading: the name of the eighth letter of the alphabet, which many British speakers famously leave unsaid at the start of words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping your aitches' is the British phrase for not sounding the H, as in 'ouse for house'; the clue is the scolding a teacher might give.
explanation.definitionFit: The spelled-out name of the letter H is what people are told not to drop in speech.

clue.text: Fear of father taking note

indicators.note: taking means holding on to, so the first word takes the second inside it

blocks.note: informal word for father
the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A child is afraid of their father noticing something.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the second note in do-re-mi.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is great fear or apprehension about something to come, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Carrying out schedule inside

blocks.note: doing a task is carrying it out
to time something is to schedule it

explanation.surface: Someone carries out a timetable while indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside looks like a container signal but is the definition: slang for being in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing time is the idiom for serving a prison sentence, and being inside is slang for being jailed.

clue.text: Clumsy, chaotic — I'm shafted!

indicators.note: chaotic means in disorder, so the letters that follow are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A bumbling, disorderly person complains that they have been cheated.
explanation.walkthrough: Shafted is British slang for treated unfairly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham-fisted describes someone awkward and heavy-handed, lacking dexterity, which is clumsy.

clue.text: It was said guys rejected broadcast

indicators.note: was said points to how the phrase sounds when spoken rather than how it is spelt

blocks.note: guys are men, and rejected means shunned; said together the phrase becomes one word

explanation.surface: A report claims some men were turned away from a broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It was said' looks like the definition, but it is the sound signal; the definition is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something broadcast has been made known publicly, and something mentioned has been spoken of or made known.

clue.text: Understand the subtlety of kit Athena's thrown out

indicators.note: things thrown out are scattered, so these letters land in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone grasps the meaning behind a goddess's gear being discarded.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of Athena's is read as 'is', linking fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a hint is to pick up on an indirect suggestion, grasping what was implied subtly.

clue.text: Pro offer Ned rejected is not allowed

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the name is written in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to be pro something is to be for it
a bid is an offer, as at auction
taken as written

explanation.surface: A professional's offer to someone called Ned is turned down as against the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Pro looks like a professional, but here it is the opposite of con.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forbidden is prohibited or banned, which is exactly not permitted.

clue.text: Refuse female almost deliriously

indicators.note: someone delirious is wildly confused, so the preceding word's letters are scrambled

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for female
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman nearly says no in a feverish frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: Refuse reads as the verb, to say no, but it is the noun meaning rubbish; almost is fodder, not a deletion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Flotsam is floating wreckage and debris, so it is rubbish or waste material.

clue.text: Some snake danced — not 20!

indicators.note: some means a portion, so only part of the following words is wanted

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A snake performs a dance, apparently without any clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 refers to the answer at 20 down, DRESSED, so 'not 20' is its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Being naked means wearing no clothing, the opposite of being clothed or covered up.

clue.text: Covered crab or salad?

definitions.note: describes the dishes rather than meaning them

blocks.note: first meaning: wearing clothes
second meaning: the word for a crab cleaned and served in its shell, or a salad with its oil and vinegar added

explanation.surface: Is the covered dish a crab or a salad?
explanation.definitionFit: To be clothed is to be covered, and a crab or salad prepared with its sauce or garnish is described the same way.

clue.text: Turn back to secure victory that is due

indicators.note: back means the word is written going backwards
to secure something is to hold it firmly, so it is wrapped around what follows

blocks.note: a go is a turn in a game
a win is a victory

explanation.surface: A player takes their turn again to clinch a victory they deserve.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn back looks like a single verb but is a noun with its reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Money owing is money still to be paid, which is money due.

clue.text: In Calais lessons could be British?

definitions.note: an example: completes the British Isles

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: found across the end of the port's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether classes taken in the French port of Calais count as British.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals the definition is a completion: the British Isles.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Isles are the island group comprising Britain, Ireland and the smaller nearby islands.

clue.text: Remove a timeline accidentally

indicators.note: something done accidentally is muddled by chance, so the letters fall into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone deletes a project's schedule by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: To eliminate is to get rid of or take away completely, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Probably am there ahead of schedule

definitions.note: a cryptic hint: a.m. hours are probably early

blocks.note: first meaning: a time marked a.m. is likely to be in the first part of the day
second meaning: arriving before the appointed time

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they will probably arrive before the expected time.
explanation.walkthrough: Am looks like the verb 'I am', but it is a.m., the morning hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Early means arriving before the due time, and the morning hours marked a.m. come at the start of the day.

clue.text: Time spell without any border force

indicators.note: with no border means the edges are trimmed away, leaving just the inner letters of each word

blocks.note: taken as written, then its outer letters go
taken as written, then its outer letters go

explanation.surface: A sentence or a magic spell is described as having no edges.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or push someone into action, which is to force them.

clue.text: Surprisingly, Noel or Sid keep at it

indicators.note: surprisingly means in an unexpected way, so the letters turn up in an unexpected order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Against expectations, either Noel or Sid perseveres.
explanation.definitionFit: To soldier on is the idiom for carrying on doggedly despite difficulty, which is persevering.

clue.text: Aches starting? Probably analgesia is needed soon

indicators.note: starting points to where each word begins, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: As aches begin, someone will probably need painkillers before long.
explanation.walkthrough: Analgesia means pain relief.
explanation.definitionFit: Pains and aches are both physical discomfort, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Proficiency of PM snatching disturbed rest

blocks.note: Theresa May, a former British Prime Minister
taken as written

clue.text: Mixed luddite cocktail
